title: Samsung R95H TV Unveils Revolutionary RGB LED Backlight Technology – The Verge Review
body:
Samsung has unveiled its newest flagship, the 95‑inch R95H, a premium television that pushes the limits of colour accuracy and brightness with a full‑array RGB LED backlight system. The model, aimed at high‑end home‑theatre enthusiasts and professional visual creators, promises a matte‑finish panel capable of reproducing an unprecedented range of hues, while delivering the deep blacks and uniform illumination that have become hallmarks of the brand’s QLED line‑up. Early hands‑on impressions suggest the R95H could set a new benchmark for consumer‑grade RGB LED displays, challenging both OLED and traditional LCD competitors in the premium segment.

At the heart of the R95H is Samsung’s proprietary “RGB‑Full Array” backlight, which replaces the conventional white‑light LEDs with three distinct clusters of red, green and blue diodes. By controlling each colour channel independently across the entire screen, the TV can generate over one billion shades, a figure that dwarfs the roughly 16‑million colour possibilities of standard LCD panels. This granular control also enables higher peak brightness—up to 2,000 nits in certain HDR formats—while preserving detail in both highlights and shadows. The matte‑type surface, a departure from the glossy finishes typical of many large‑screen TVs, reduces glare and reflections, making the R95H suitable for bright living rooms as well as dimly lit home‑cinema setups.

The R95H’s visual prowess is complemented by a suite of processing technologies designed to maximise the raw potential of the RGB backlight. Samsung’s Neo Quantum Processor 8K upscales lower‑resolution content to near‑native 8K fidelity, using AI‑driven algorithms to reconstruct fine details and suppress artefacts. Meanwhile, the company’s “Quantum Dot” colour‑enhancement layer further widens the colour gamut, ensuring that the expanded palette from the backlight translates into vivid, lifelike images. The TV also supports a full range of HDR standards—including HDR10+, Dolby Vision and HLG—allowing content creators and streaming services to deliver their most demanding productions without compromise.

Industry analysts see the R95H as a strategic response to the growing dominance of OLED panels, which have long been praised for their perfect blacks and infinite contrast ratios but suffer from brightness limitations and potential burn‑in issues. By delivering comparable contrast with a backlight that can exceed OLED’s peak luminance, Samsung hopes to attract buyers who value both high dynamic range and colour fidelity without the longevity concerns of organic displays. Moreover, the matte coating addresses a common criticism of glossy panels: susceptibility to ambient light reflections that can wash out colours in well‑lit environments. This combination of brightness, colour depth, and anti‑glare treatment positions the R95H as a compelling alternative for consumers who prioritize versatility across varied lighting conditions.

Pricing and availability will be decisive factors in the R95H’s market impact. Samsung has positioned the model in the ultra‑premium tier, with a launch price expected to hover around $7,500–$8,000 USD, placing it squarely against high‑end OLED offerings from competing manufacturers. Early adopters, particularly cinephiles and professional video editors, may find the investment justified by the TV’s ability to render colour‑critical work with unprecedented accuracy. For the broader consumer base, the cost could be a barrier, especially as 8K content remains limited and many households continue to stream 4K material. Nonetheless, Samsung’s decision to push the envelope in RGB LED technology signals a commitment to diversifying the premium display landscape beyond OLED.

Looking ahead, the R95H could serve as a blueprint for the next generation of high‑performance LCDs. If Samsung’s RGB‑Full Array proves reliable and scalable, we may see similar backlight architectures trickle down to mid‑range models, gradually narrowing the gap between premium and mainstream offerings. As streaming services expand their HDR libraries and content creators adopt higher‑resolution workflows, demand for displays that can faithfully reproduce a wider colour spectrum will only intensify. Samsung’s latest flagship therefore not only showcases a technological milestone but also hints at an evolving market where multiple display technologies coexist, each catering to distinct use cases and consumer preferences.
